units.text: A minimalist text art studio where users paste prose and transform it into interactive word-based visualizations.
Saved pieces persist in a local SQLite database through Echo's Express API.
Words are humanity's primary mechanism for understanding one another.
Language carries emotion, memory, identity, intention.
Yet modern communication increasingly prioritizes speed over reflection — compressing meaning into fragments, captions, messages, and signals.
In trying to communicate faster, we often lose the emotional weight that language once carried.
Echo was created as a response to that loss.
Echo transforms writing into living visual systems that continue evolving after the sentence itself ends.
Instead of treating text as static information, Echo interprets language as movement: words cluster, drift, repeat, orbit, fragment, and reform over time.
Each form gives language a different kind of afterlife.
Maps relationships between connected ideas and recurring language patterns.
Disperses words into atmospheric fields that move like memory.
Compresses language into typographic residue and monochrome traces.
Pulls repeated language into motion, recurrence, and collapse.
Organizes words around semantic anchors and emotional weight.
I wanted better feedback on my own poetry.
Most AI writing tools gave me the same thing: vague praise, generic craft advice, and a chat box that treated a poem like a support ticket.
They could count my repetitions.
They rarely told me what the draft was about.
MuseLab is my attempt to fix that—for myself and for anyone else who writes in short forms.
You submit a draft.
The backend reads it through several lenses (structure, emotion, metaphor, development, references).
The UI returns a dossier: folio tabs you flip through, not a conversation you scroll forever.
What makes it different: interpretation over generation.
The app is not trying to rewrite your poem.
It tries to argue about it—grounded in your lines—and leave you with something you can revise from.
Dossier, not chat.
A poem isn't a thread.
I wanted the feeling of a workshop packet—sheets you move through at your own pace.
Interpretation, not replacement.
Agents name mechanisms in your language so you can revise.
I explicitly did not want here's my version of your poem.
Hybrid analysis, not LLM-only.
Deterministic features, an emotion classifier, and reference retrieval run before the language-model agents.
That grounding keeps feedback from floating off into generic advice.
Two agent systems, kept separate.
Poetry agents critique your text.
Builder agents critique this repo.
Mixing those prompts would blur the product.
Humans stay in the loop on builder output.
Builder agents write markdown reports.
They do not merge code.
I review, edit, reject, then implement.

Differ is a platform for reasoning about contextual differences in human experience design — built on the idea that the same context-aware experience can mean something different depending on who encounters it and where.

It takes a machine-interpretable definition of an experience and returns a set of visualizations that surface where that experience might break down for particular populations or settings, before a designer ships it.
Four core computational abstractions: concept expressions, accountable perspectives, issues of concern, and visualizations.
Accountable perspectives capture meaning differences across geography (urban/rural, state, neighborhood), demographics (age, budget, wheelchair accessibility), and setting (time of day).
Issue functions score a given perspective for prevalence, conceptual fit, popularity, safety, and affordability.
Reference systems combine Yelp and Foursquare data, public crime datasets, neighborhood data, and census data; visualizations are generated with geopandas and Plotly.
First author on the CHI 2026 submission presenting Differ alongside real-world case studies.

The project grew out of Northwestern's Design, Technology, and Research course inside the Delta Lab, and turned into something I kept building for almost two years: a lightweight data analysis framework that connects how a person expresses a concept to how a machine interprets it, aimed at surfacing actionable insight for designers working on inclusive, context-aware systems.

The case studies in the CHI submission use real-world reference systems rather than synthetic data, which is most of why the project took as long as it did — a difference that only shows up across actual Chicago neighborhoods is a much harder thing to render responsibly than one that shows up in a toy dataset.
Routing queries through a multi-agent Langflow system wrapped around an internal retrieval-augmented generation pipeline.

I worked inside an internal AI platform built around retrieval-augmented generation — the kind of system meant to let people ask plain questions of dense, hierarchical document sets and get back something trustworthy.

My main contribution was a multi-agent system in Langflow that sat in front of the RAG pipeline, routing each incoming query between a retrieval agent and a conversational agent depending on what the question actually needed, with translation and response post-processing layered on top.
The rest of the internship split between two things that don't usually share a sentence: evaluation logic and rendering bugs.

I wrote backend evaluation code for the RAG prototypes to check whether the system was retrieving the right documents and producing answers worth trusting, and separately tracked down full-stack bugs where deeply nested, hierarchical data was breaking the frontend's rendering logic and causing cascading UI failures.
Fixing both halves taught the same lesson twice: what makes an AI feature feel reliable usually has nothing to do with the model.
I design systems that move between computation, language, and human judgment.
